title: The Way, the Truth, and the Life; the Promise of the Advocate
summary: Jesus comforts his troubled disciples: he is going to prepare a place for them in his Father's house and will come back for them. He tells Thomas that he is the way and the truth and the life, and tells Philip that whoever has seen him has seen the Father. He promises another Advocate, the Spirit of truth, who will be with them and teach them, says that he and the Father will make their home with those who love him, and leaves them his peace before rising to go.
story:
Jesus has just told the disciples that he is leaving, that one of them will betray him, and that Peter will deny him (13:21-38). Chapter 14 answers their fear. It opens and nearly closes with the same words, “Do not let your hearts be troubled” (14:1, 14:27), and the whole chapter explains why his going away is for their good: he goes to prepare a place, he will come back, the Father will send the Spirit, the Father and the Son will make their home with those who love him, and his peace will remain.

Questions from Thomas, Philip, and Judas (not Iscariot) move the conversation along. Each reveals how little the disciples yet understand, and each draws out more of who Jesus is: the way to the Father, the one in whom the Father is seen, the one who will show himself to those who love him. The chapter looks beyond the cross in three directions at once. Jesus speaks of coming back for his disciples at the end (14:3), of seeing them again after a little while (14:19), which points to the resurrection, and of coming to them through the Spirit (14:18, 14:23). By its end the reader has heard the first of five sayings about the Advocate (14:16-17, 14:26, 15:26, 16:7-11, 16:13-15), and Jesus rises, saying “Let us go on from here” (14:31), toward the hour that the prince of this world thinks is his.
historical:
The setting is still the meal on the night before Jesus' death, in Jerusalem at Passover time. Jesus' words take the form of a farewell speech, a pattern well known in Israel's Scriptures and in later Jewish writing. Jacob blesses his sons before his death (Genesis 49), Moses delivers the whole book of Deuteronomy as a farewell, Joshua (Joshua 23 to 24), Samuel (1 Samuel 12), and David (1 Kings 2:1-9, 1 Chronicles 28 to 29) give final charges, and the dying Mattathias exhorts his sons to zeal for the law (1 Maccabees 2:49-70). Jewish works from the centuries around Jesus' time develop the form: Jubilees 22 gives Abraham's last words to Jacob, the Testament of Moses retells Moses' charge to Joshua, and the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs imagine the final words of each of Jacob's sons (in the form we have them, they have passed through Christian hands, and their date is debated). Such speeches typically announce the leader's departure, comfort the followers, recall his example, give commands, warn of trouble, promise blessing, and name a successor. John's farewell discourse has all these features, with two differences no other farewell has: the one who departs promises to come back, and the successor is the Spirit of God, who will make the departed one present.

The Greek world knew the form too. Plato's Phaedo tells of Socrates' last day in 399 BC, conversing with his friends about the immortality of the soul before drinking the hemlock, and it says that his friends felt as though they were losing a father and would spend the rest of their lives as orphans (Phaedo 116a). Jesus' promise, I will not leave you as orphans (14:18), speaks into exactly that fear.

The three questioners are among the less prominent disciples. Thomas, called Didymus, the Twin (11:16, 20:24), speaks with blunt realism here as he does before Lazarus's tomb and after the resurrection. Philip, from Bethsaida (1:44), had been tested by Jesus over the feeding of the crowd (6:5-7) and had brought the Greeks' request (12:21-22). The Judas who is not Iscariot appears in Luke's lists of the Twelve as Judas of James (Luke 6:16, Acts 1:13); Matthew and Mark name Thaddaeus in the corresponding place (Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18), and many identify the two.

The language of the chapter also has parallels in Jewish writings of the period. The Community Rule from Qumran speaks of two spirits in which humanity walks, a spirit of truth and a spirit of deceit (1QS 3:18-19, 4:21-23), and the phrase spirit of truth also appears in the Testament of Judah (20:1-5). John's Spirit of truth is not one of two opposed spirits within people but the Spirit of God, sent by the Father in Jesus' name, whom the world cannot receive. The world in this chapter (14:17, 14:19, 14:22, 14:27, 14:30, 14:31) does not mean the created earth or any one nation. In John it usually means human society organized in rejection of God, which God nonetheless loves (3:16), and its prince (14:30, as at 12:31 and 16:11) is the devil. Jewish and Roman authorities alike will act on the world's behalf in the chapters that follow.
cultural:
“In My Father’s house are many rooms” (14:2) would bring two pictures to mind. One is the family household, the father's house (Hebrew bet av) in which sons and their families lived together, sometimes in rooms built around a shared courtyard. The other is the temple, which Jesus had called “My Father’s house” in 2:16 and which had many chambers around its courts (1 Kings 6:5, Ezekiel 41:5-6). The word for rooms, monē, means a place to stay, a dwelling, from the verb menō, to remain or abide, and John uses the same noun when Jesus says he and the Father will make their home with the one who loves him (14:23). Some readers explain the promise from a Jewish wedding custom, in which the groom prepared a room in his father's house and then came to fetch the bride. The image is attractive, but the details are drawn from much later sources and are not needed to understand the text, which is about belonging to the Father's household.

The King James Version's ‘many mansions’ comes through William Tyndale's translation (1526) from the Latin Vulgate's mansiones, which meant dwellings or stopping places. In older English a mansion was simply a place to live, not a grand house; the modern sense has sometimes given the verse an image of heavenly real estate that the Greek does not carry.

Peace (Hebrew shalom) was the ordinary Jewish greeting and farewell, and it meant more than calm: wholeness, well-being, and right relationship with God and others. Jesus uses the ordinary farewell, then says that his peace is not given as the world gives (14:27). The Roman world celebrated the Pax Romana, the peace Augustus and his successors claimed to have brought by conquest, and the disciples would soon see that peace enforced by crucifixion. To be left as orphans (14:18) was a picture of helplessness; the Law repeatedly names the orphan among those God protects (Exodus 22:22, Deuteronomy 10:18), and disciples whose teacher died could be described as orphaned, as Plato describes Socrates' friends.

The word paraklētos was used in Greek for someone called to stand beside another, especially an advocate or supporter in a court of law, though not usually a paid professional lawyer. The word was borrowed into Hebrew and Aramaic as praqlit, and the Mishnah says that whoever performs one commandment gains for himself one advocate, and whoever commits one transgression gains one accuser (m. Avot 4:11). The idea of asking or acting in someone's name belongs to the world of agency, where a messenger acts with his sender's authority; the Mishnah's principle that a man's agent is like himself (m. Berakhot 5:5) captures it. Asking in Jesus' name is asking as his representatives, in keeping with his purposes. Philip's request to see the Father recalls Moses, who asked to see God's glory and was told that no one may see God's face and live (Exodus 33:18-23), and the elders of Israel who saw the God of Israel on the mountain (Exodus 24:9-11). John has already said that no one has ever seen God, but the only Son has made him known (1:18).
literary:
The chapter is dialogue that becomes monologue. Thomas (14:5), Philip (14:8), and Judas (14:22) each ask a question that shows a misunderstanding, and Jesus' answers carry the teaching forward. The pattern is common in John (Nicodemus in chapter 3, the Samaritan woman in chapter 4), and here it lets the reader overhear the disciples' confusion and see it met. The sixth of the Gospel's seven I am sayings with a predicate stands near the start: “I am the way and the truth and the life” (14:6), following the bread (6:35), the light (8:12), the door (10:7), the good shepherd (10:11), and the resurrection and the life (11:25), and preceding the true vine (15:1).

The chapter is framed by an inclusio, Do not let your hearts be troubled (14:1, 14:27), and its themes circle and return in a spiral typical of John: going and coming, loving and keeping commandments, the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, believing because of the works, the gift of the Spirit. The logic moves outward: the Son is in the Father and the Father in him (14:10-11), then the disciples will know that the Son is in the Father, they in him, and he in them (14:20), and finally the Father and the Son will come and make their home with the one who loves him (14:23). The first Advocate saying (14:16-17) calls the Spirit another Advocate, implying that Jesus has been the first; the second (14:26) says the Spirit will teach and remind, which explains how the disciples' later remembering, noted at 2:22 and 12:16, came about.

The coming of Jesus in this chapter has more than one reference. I will come back (14:3) most naturally refers to his return at the end; I will come to you and you will see me (14:18-19) refers to the resurrection appearances; and the Father and the Son coming to make their home with the believer (14:23) is fulfilled through the Spirit. C. H. Dodd's reading of John stressed the present fulfillment, while other interpreters, Raymond Brown among them, hold that John keeps the future hope alongside the present gift and lets the senses overlap.

Jesus' last words, “Get up! Let us go on from here” (14:31), are followed by three more chapters of teaching, and 18:1 finally says that he went out with his disciples. Rudolf Bultmann rearranged the discourse so that chapters 15 to 17 came before 13:36 to 14:31. Many scholars, among them Raymond Brown, think chapters 15 to 17 gather further discourse material added at a later stage of the Gospel's composition, so that 14:31 once led straight to 18:1. Others, such as D. A. Carson, think Jesus and the disciples left the room and he kept teaching on the way, and still others read the words as a turning to face what is coming rather than a change of place. The canonical order is the only form of the Gospel we have, and it reads as a deliberate whole.

outline.t: Many rooms in the Father's house
Thomas: I am the way and the truth and the life
Philip: whoever has seen me has seen the Father
Another Advocate, the Spirit of truth
The Spirit will teach; my peace I give you

doctrines.note: Jesus promises “another Advocate to be with you forever” (14:16), the Spirit of truth who abides with the disciples and will be in them (14:17), and who will teach them all things and remind them of everything Jesus said (14:26). The Spirit is personal, sent by the Father in the Son's name, and continues Jesus' own presence with his people. The chapter is foundational for the doctrine that the Spirit guided the apostles' memory and teaching.

The chapter speaks of Father, Son, and Spirit as distinct and yet inseparable: the Father dwells in the Son and does his works (14:10), the Son asks the Father (14:16), the Father sends the Spirit in the Son's name (14:26), and the Father and the Son come to make their home with believers (14:23). The fourth-century church read “the Father is greater than I” (14:28) as speaking of the Son's relation to the Father as his source, or of his humble state in the incarnation, not of a lesser divine nature; see the hard questions.

“On that day you will know that I am in My Father, and you are in Me, and I am in you” (14:20). The mutual indwelling of the Father and the Son becomes the pattern for the believer's union with Christ, and the promise that the Father and the Son will make their home with the one who loves Jesus (14:23) describes that union as God's presence dwelling in his people.

“Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father” (14:9). Jesus is the full and personal revelation of God. What God is like is not guessed at from a distance but seen in the words and works of Jesus, which are the Father's words and works (14:10). The chapter answers the longing of Moses and Philip to see God with a person.

“I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am” (14:3). The chapter's first promise is Jesus' return to take his people to himself, and the goal of that hope is personal: to be where he is. The same chapter speaks of his coming in the resurrection and through the Spirit, so the future hope and the present gift belong together.

words.note: Paraklētos, Advocate, Helper, Counselor, or Comforter; translations vary because the word covers several roles. It occurs five times in the New Testament, four in John's farewell discourse for the Holy Spirit (14:16, 14:26, 15:26, 16:7) and once in 1 John 2:1 for Jesus, our advocate with the Father. Its root sense is one called alongside, and in Greek it most often meant a legal advocate or supporter; BDAG gives one who appears in another's behalf, mediator, intercessor, helper. The older rendering Comforter, used in the English Bibles of the Reformation era, comes from a time when comfort still carried the sense of strengthen. When Jesus says another Advocate, he implies that he has been the first.

Hodos, way, road, path. It occurs about 101 times in the New Testament and four times in John (1:23, 14:4, 14:5, 14:6). In the Old Testament the way of the Lord describes both how God acts and how his people should live (Psalm 25:4-5, Isaiah 40:3, which John quotes at 1:23). Thomas asks for directions to a place, and Jesus answers that he himself is the way. The earliest Christians were known as followers of the Way (Acts 9:2, 24:14).

Alētheia, truth. It occurs about 109 times in the New Testament and 25 times in John's Gospel, more than in any other book. In John truth is not only accurate statement but the reality of God made known, which comes through Jesus (1:17), which sets free (8:32), and which Jesus is (14:6). The Spirit is the Spirit of truth (14:17), and Pilate will ask what truth is while it stands before him (18:38).

Monē, dwelling place, room, a place to stay, from the verb menō, to remain or abide. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, both in this chapter: for the many rooms in the Father's house (14:2) and for the home the Father and the Son will make with the one who loves Jesus (14:23). The link suggests that the future dwelling with God and the present indwelling of God belong together. Irenaeus and other early readers took the monai as different dwellings or degrees of reward, but the word itself means simply dwelling places.

Orphanos, orphan, one bereft of parents or protector. It occurs twice in the New Testament (John 14:18, James 1:27). The Greek Old Testament uses it for the fatherless whom God defends (Exodus 22:22, Psalm 68:5). “I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you” (14:18) assures the disciples that Jesus' going will not leave them alone: he will come to them in the resurrection and through the Spirit, and in him they have a Father (20:17).

Eirēnē, peace. It occurs about 92 times in the New Testament and six times in John (14:27 twice, 16:33, 20:19, 20:21, 20:26). In the Greek Old Testament it translates shalom, which means wholeness and well-being in right relation with God. Jesus leaves peace as a farewell gift (14:27) and gives it again as the risen Lord's greeting (20:19). It is peace in the middle of trouble, not the absence of trouble (16:33).

Tarassō, to stir up, trouble, unsettle. It occurs 17 times in the New Testament. John uses it of the stirred water at Bethesda (5:7) and three times of Jesus himself, deeply troubled at Lazarus's tomb (11:33), at the coming of the hour (12:27), and at the betrayal (13:21). When Jesus tells the disciples not to let their hearts be troubled (14:1, 14:27), he is not asking them to feel nothing; the one who says it has been troubled himself and has gone through it trusting the Father.

Emphanizō, to make visible, reveal, disclose; in legal contexts, to present evidence or lay charges. It occurs ten times in the New Testament, five of them in Acts in the legal sense. In John it appears only here: Jesus will reveal himself to the one who loves him (14:21), and Judas asks why he will reveal himself to the disciples and not to the world (14:22). Judas expects a public manifestation like a messianic triumph; Jesus answers with a personal and relational disclosure to those who love him and keep his word.

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as the only way to the Father because he is the one who has come from the Father and shares his life. He does not say he knows the way or teaches the way, but that he is the way, and the truth and the life with it. Thomas's question is about geography; Jesus' answer is about a person. The Old Testament longed to see God: Moses asked to see his glory (Exodus 33:18), the psalmists sought his face (Psalm 27:8), and Isaiah saw the Lord enthroned (Isaiah 6:1). Philip's request gathers that longing, and Jesus answers that it is met in him. His words and works are the Father's words and works (14:10), which is why seeing him is seeing the Father.

He is also the giver of the Spirit and the one who comes. The prophets promised that God would put his Spirit within his people (Ezekiel 36:27) and dwell among them (Ezekiel 37:27, Zechariah 2:10); Jesus promises that the Father will send the Spirit to be in the disciples (14:17), and that the Father and the Son will make their home with them (14:23). The God who tabernacled with Israel and whose glory dwelt in the Word made flesh (1:14) will dwell in his people.

The chapter shows Christ as the obedient Son. He goes to the cross not because the prince of this world has any claim on him (14:30) but so that the world may know that he loves the Father and does exactly what the Father commanded (14:31). His death is an act of love and obedience, not of defeat. And it shows his care for his friends on the night of his own suffering. Facing betrayal and death, he spends his last hours comforting them, praying for them, and promising them a place, a helper, and his peace. Because he lives, they will live also (14:19): the resurrection life of Jesus is the ground of the believer's life.
interpretation:
The chapter has been one of the most read in the church. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.36.2) cited the elders' teaching that the many rooms mean different dwellings for the saved according to their fruitfulness, some in heaven, some in paradise, and some in the city. Augustine's Tractates on John 67 to 79 cover the chapter; in Tractate 67 he reconciles the many rooms with the single denarius paid to every laborer in the parable of the vineyard: eternal life is one and the same for all, while the rooms are the different degrees of glory within it. John Chrysostom's homilies on the chapter, beginning with Homily 73, dwell on Jesus' comfort of disciples shaken by the prediction of Peter's denial.

The Arian controversy of the fourth century made 14:28 a battleground. Arians and later Eunomians cited “the Father is greater than I” as proof that the Son was a lesser being. Gregory of Nazianzus (Oration 30.7) answered that the Father is greater as the cause or source of the Son, not in nature, and Augustine (On the Trinity 1.7.14) that the Son is less than the Father in the form of a servant he took, while equal to him in the form of God. The verses on the Spirit sent by the Father in the Son's name (14:16, 14:26) later featured, alongside 15:26, in the long debate between East and West over the Spirit's procession.

Thomas Aquinas's commentary on John reads 14:6 christologically: Christ is the way according to his humanity and the truth and the life, the goal, according to his divinity, so that in him the way and the destination are one. Thomas à Kempis built a chapter of The Imitation of Christ (book 3, chapter 56) on the verse, as the way to be followed, the truth to be believed, and the life to be hoped for. Martin Luther's sermons on John 14 to 16, preached in the late 1530s, treat the chapter as a defense of Christ's deity and a comfort against terror of conscience. Calvin's commentary on 14:28 reads it neither of the divine nature nor simply of the human, but of Christ in his office as mediator, in the lowly state from which he was going to the Father's glory.

Modern debate over 14:6 has centered on religious pluralism. John Hick (God Has Many Names, 1980) argued for a pluralism in which the great religions are different responses to one ultimate reality. Clark Pinnock (A Wideness in God's Mercy, 1992) defended an inclusivism in which Christ alone saves but may save some who have not heard of him, and the Second Vatican Council's Lumen Gentium 16 (1964) affirmed that those who through no fault of their own do not know the gospel but seek God sincerely may be saved, a position Karl Rahner developed in his idea of anonymous Christians. Ronald Nash (Is Jesus the Only Savior?, 1994) defended the view that explicit faith is required, and Lesslie Newbigin (The Gospel in a Pluralist Society, 1989) argued for the uniqueness of Christ as public truth while declining to limit God's mercy by speculation. The Jewish philosopher Franz Rosenzweig, in The Star of Redemption (1921), accepted the verse for the nations, who come to the Father through the Son, while holding that Israel does not need to come to the Father because it is already with him.

In worship, 14:1-6 is among the passages most often read at Christian funerals and appears among the Gospel readings for the burial service in the Episcopal Church's Book of Common Prayer (1979). The Revised Common Lectionary reads 14:1-14 on the fifth Sunday of Easter and 14:15-21 on the sixth Sunday of Easter in Year A, 14:23-29 on the sixth Sunday of Easter in Year C, and 14:8-17 (with 25-27) on the Day of Pentecost in Year C. George Herbert's poem The Call, from The Temple (1633), turns 14:6 into a prayer to Christ as way, truth, and life, and Ralph Vaughan Williams set it as the fourth of his Five Mystical Songs, first performed in 1911.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles here come from the manuscripts and from punctuation. In verse 2 the best manuscripts include the word that (hoti) after If it were not so, would I have told you. With it, the sentence is most naturally a question, If it were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you? (BSB, ESV, NIV). Without it, as in the later text, it reads as two statements, ‘if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you’ (KJV). In verse 4 the earliest manuscripts read a short sentence, literally ‘and where I am going, you know the way’; later manuscripts expand it to ‘whither I go ye know, and the way ye know’ (KJV).

In verse 7 the manuscripts divide between a rebuke and a promise. Many, followed by the BSB and ESV, read ‘If you had known Me, you would know My Father as well’, implying the disciples had not truly known him. Others, including Papyrus 66 and Codex Sinaiticus, read ‘If you have known me, you will know my Father also’, a promise; the Nestle-Aland edition prints this reading. In verse 14 a few manuscripts and early versions omit the whole verse, perhaps because it seemed to repeat verse 13, and others omit Me in ask Me, perhaps because praying to Jesus rather than to the Father seemed unusual; most modern editions include both. In verse 15 the best text reads a future, you will keep my commandments, while the later text reads an imperative, ‘keep my commandments’ (KJV). In verse 17 manuscripts divide between will be in you (future, as in the BSB) and is in you (present), a difference that bears on whether the indwelling of the Spirit is promised or already begun.

There are also translation differences. The KJV's ‘many mansions’ (verse 2) and ‘Comforter’ (verses 16 and 26) are older renderings of words modern versions translate rooms or dwelling places, and Advocate, Helper, or Counselor. In verse 1 the Greek verb believe can be read as a statement or a command in both clauses; hence ‘ye believe in God, believe also in me’ (KJV), You believe in God; believe in Me as well (BSB), or ‘Believe in God; believe also in me’ (ESV).

teach.big: Jesus meets his disciples' fear of abandonment by showing that his going brings them to the Father: he is the way to the Father, the one in whom the Father is seen, and the giver of the Spirit through whom the Father and the Son come to dwell with those who love him.

outline.t: The cure for a troubled heart is trust in Jesus as in God, and a promise that his going is a going ahead to prepare a place with the Father.
Jesus does not give directions to God; he is the way, and to know him is to know the Father.
The longing to see God is met in the face, words, and works of Jesus, and his works give reasons for faith.
Jesus' departure launches his followers' mission, and prayer in his name serves the Father's glory in the Son.
Love for Jesus shows itself in keeping his commands, and the Spirit of truth is given to be with his people forever.
Jesus will not leave his people orphaned; through resurrection and Spirit, the Father and the Son make their home with those who love him.
The Spirit teaches and reminds, grounding the church's memory of Jesus in his own promise.
Jesus leaves a peace the world cannot give and walks toward the cross in free obedience and love for the Father.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first turns the Father's house into a promise of luxury, helped by the older word mansions. The rooms mean belonging and presence: the goal is to be where Jesus is (14:3). The second builds a doctrine of heaven out of a first-century Jewish wedding custom that the text does not mention and that rests on much later sources.

With 14:6, avoid two opposite errors. One wields it as a weapon, forgetting that it was spoken as comfort to frightened friends on the night before Jesus died. The other softens it into one path among many, which the context will not allow. Teach what the verse claims, that Jesus himself is the way to the Father, and be honest that Christians differ on what it implies for those who never hear of him.

With 14:13-14, do not treat whatever you ask in my name as a blank check or a formula that guarantees answers if the right words are said. Asking in his name means asking as his representatives, for what serves the Father's glory in the Son. With 14:12, greater works does not mean more spectacular miracles than Jesus' own; most interpreters understand it of the scope of the church's mission after the resurrection, reaching the nations through the Spirit. With 14:15, do not make obedience the price of Jesus' love; it is the evidence of love for him. And with 14:28, do not use the Father is greater to teach that the Son is a lesser being, a reading the church rejected in the fourth century.
teach.pastoral: This chapter is read at funerals and bedside vigils more than almost any other, so teach it knowing that grief will be in the room. The promise of a place with the Father and of Jesus coming back comforts because it is personal, not because it answers every question about death. Do not use Do not let your hearts be troubled to shame the anxious or the grieving; Jesus says it after being troubled himself (11:33, 12:27, 13:21), and his remedy is his presence, not a demand to feel differently. People who have lost a parent, or who grew up without a father, may hear I will not leave you as orphans with particular force; let it stand as the promise it is. For those who struggle with doubt, Jesus' words to Philip, believe on account of the works themselves (14:11), show that he welcomes faith that needs reasons.

hard.q: Isn't it narrow and arrogant for Jesus to say that no one comes to the Father except through him?
hard.a:
Many thoughtful people find 14:6 the most offensive verse in the Gospel, since it seems to dismiss the sincere faith of others. The pluralist form of the objection was stated by John Hick (God Has Many Names, 1980; An Interpretation of Religion, 1989): the great religions produce comparable saints and are culturally shaped responses to one ultimate reality, so no one tradition can claim to be the only way. Critical scholars add that the verse reflects the Johannine community's conflict with the synagogue late in the first century rather than words of the historical Jesus. Jewish readers have their own concern, since the verse was long used to deny that Jews have any relationship with God; Franz Rosenzweig (The Star of Redemption, 1921) answered by accepting the verse for the nations while holding that Israel is already with the Father and so does not need to come to him.

Several responses have been made. The claim is offered on the night of Jesus' death, to frightened friends, as comfort that there is a way to God, not as a boast. It also follows from what John says Jesus is: if he is the Word who was with God and was God (1:1), then coming to the Father through him is coming to God through God, not through a rival. Lesslie Newbigin (The Gospel in a Pluralist Society, 1989) argued that pluralism itself makes an exclusive claim about ultimate reality, and that the Christian confession of Christ as the truth is public truth to be offered humbly to all. The question is less whether the claim is narrow than whether it is true: a merely human teacher saying it would be arrogant, but the Gospel's case is that Jesus is not merely a human teacher.

Christians have held different views about what the verse implies for those who never hear of Jesus. Some, such as Ronald Nash (Is Jesus the Only Savior?, 1994), hold that explicit faith in Christ is necessary for salvation. Others, such as Clark Pinnock (A Wideness in God's Mercy, 1992) and, in Catholic teaching, Lumen Gentium 16, hold that Christ may save some who respond to the light they have without knowing his name. A minority hope that all will finally be saved through him. All of these are views about how Christ saves, not about whether salvation comes through him, and they differ on a question the church has not settled with one voice.

hard.q: If the Father is greater than Jesus (14:28), how can Jesus be fully God?
hard.a:
The objection is ancient and still pressed. Arius of Alexandria in the early fourth century, and after him Eunomius, argued that the Son is the first and greatest of God's creatures but not God in the same sense as the Father, and they cited this verse as a plain statement of the Son's inferiority. Unitarian Christians and modern groups such as Jehovah's Witnesses read it the same way, and some historical critics argue that John's Gospel, whatever its high christology, still subordinates the Son to the Father as the one sent to the sender.

The church's answers came in the fourth and fifth centuries and have been refined since. Athanasius and the Council of Nicaea (325) confessed the Son to be of one being with the Father, and the Nicene fathers read the verse accordingly. Gregory of Nazianzus (Oration 30.7) argued that the Father is greater as the cause or source of the Son, since the Son is eternally begotten of the Father, but not greater in nature; many Eastern theologians have followed him. Augustine (On the Trinity 1.7.14) read the verse of the form of a servant that the Son took in the incarnation (Philippians 2:6-7): in that form he is less than the Father, while in the form of God he is equal. Calvin read it of Christ's office as mediator in his humble state, about to return to the glory he had with the Father (17:5). These readings are not mutually exclusive, and the context supports them: Jesus says the disciples should rejoice that he is going to the Father, which fits a contrast between his present lowliness and the glory he is entering.

The same chapter holds the other side. Jesus says that whoever has seen him has seen the Father (14:9), that he is in the Father and the Father in him (14:10), that he will do whatever the disciples ask (14:14), and that he and the Father will come to make their home with believers (14:23). John's Gospel as a whole calls the Word God (1:1) and ends with Thomas's confession, My Lord and my God (20:28). The historic creeds confess that the Son is fully God and that the Father is the eternal source of the Son; how best to state the order within the Trinity remains a question Christian theologians continue to discuss within that confession.
